title: Bamidbar: teachers are parents (Numbers 3:1)
hookLine: Aaron's sons are called Moses' too; whoever teaches a child is like a parent (Sanhedrin 19b)

lines: THE ONE WHO STAYED AFTER CLASS.
A FAMILY TREE THAT LOOKS WRONG.
cards: Almost everyone can name one. The teacher who stayed after class. The coach who saw something in a kid nobody else did.
The aunt who taught you to read music, the neighbor who taught you to ride a bike, the camp counselor whose voice you still hear when you're scared. They aren't on your birth certificate.
But if someone asked who made you who you are, their names would come up fast. The Torah has a verse that seems, at first, to have made a mistake in a family tree. The rabbis decided it hadn't.

teach.b: Numbers three, verse one: "Now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses in the day that the LORD spoke with Moses in mount Sinai." You'd expect two lists of children.
Then verse two names the sons, and they're only Aaron's: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Moses' own sons aren't there. So why is the heading Aaron and Moses?
The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, page nineteen b, answers in a sentence quoted ever since. Aaron fathered them; Moses taught them. And so Scripture counts them as his.
Whoever teaches Torah to someone else's child, the Talmud says, it is as if they had given birth to that child. The same page has a sister teaching.
In the book of Samuel, some children are named as Michal's, though another woman bore them.
The Talmud explains: Michal raised them, and whoever raises an orphan in their home is counted by Scripture as the parent. Put the two together and you get a wide, generous idea of family.
Parenthood is something you do as well as something you are.
In Jewish tradition, the teacher holds a near-sacred place, and the old law codes discuss honoring one's teacher alongside honoring one's parents.
Rashi, reading this very verse, says it plainly: Moses taught them Torah, so they're called his offspring. A family tree, on this reading, has more branches than the birth records show.

how: Jewish tradition gives teachers great honor; the Talmud's teaching that whoever teaches another's child Torah is as if they gave birth to them is often quoted at teacher-appreciation events and at the close of a child's studies.

o: a teacher counted as a child's own parent

games.q: the verse promises the generations of Aaron and Moses, then names only Aaron's sons. how does the Talmud explain it?
o: Moses taught them, so they count as his.
games.why: Sanhedrin 19b: whoever teaches Torah to another's child, Scripture counts as if they gave birth to them.

practice: Think of a child in your life, your own, a niece, a student, a friend's kid, or the child you once were, and ask who taught that child something that stuck: a teacher, a coach, a babysitter, an older cousin.
Picture them, and let yourself feel grateful in a specific way: for this lesson, on that day.

wordCard.voice: Bamidbar. This week in the wilderness book: still remembered, be strong, the wilderness teaches, count every head, everyone around the center, set apart to serve, and teachers are parents too.
